---
title: "Quiz: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A predicted nucleus outline has one thin protrusion of 12 px; elsewhere it is perfect. Which changes most: IoU, average surface distance (ASD) or Hausdorff distance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of them is a maximum, which an average, which counts pixels?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Hausdorff distance: it is the worst boundary distance, so it becomes 12 px. The ASD averages over all boundary points and rises only a little; IoU counts pixels and a thin protrusion has very few.
:::

---

**Q2.** You care about the typical error of a cell outline in µm, for objects of very different sizes. Why is IoU a poor choice, and what would you use?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a one-pixel error do to the IoU of a small and of a large object?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
IoU mixes the outline error with the object size: the same 1-px error gives a much lower IoU for a small object. The average surface distance (in pixels or µm) measures the outline error directly and means the same for every size; add Hausdorff or HD95 if single large deviations matter.
:::

---

**Q3.** An automated cell count has correlation $r = 0.98$ with the manual count over 50 images. Is the method accurate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does $r$ say about the identity line?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not necessarily. $r$ only says the points lie close to some straight line; a method that always counts 70 % of the cells has $r$ close to 1. Look at the Bland–Altman plot: the bias (mean difference), the limits of agreement, and whether the difference depends on the count.
:::

---

**Q4.** In a Bland–Altman plot the differences (auto − manual) go from about 0 for sparse images to −30 for dense ones. Name a likely cause and a better way to report the agreement.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What goes wrong more often when nuclei touch?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A proportional bias: in dense images more nuclei touch and are merged, so the undercount grows with the count. One bias and one pair of limits do not describe it; report the ratio auto/manual (or the differences of logarithms) against the size, or the bias as a function of the count.
:::

---

**Q5.** Your method undercounts every image by 8 %. Does this matter when you compare treated with control wells? When would it matter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the bias depend on the condition?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A constant relative bias cancels when both conditions are measured the same way: the ratio treated/control is unchanged. It matters for absolute numbers (cells per mm²), and when the bias depends on the condition, e.g. if the treatment makes the cells denser and the method merges more of them there.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two expert annotators agree with F1 0.85 at $\tau = 0.5$. A new method scores 0.87 against one of them. What is a fair summary?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the ceiling of any score against one annotator?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The method agrees with that annotator about as well as another expert does: "as good as a human annotator", within the uncertainty of both numbers. It is not "better than humans"; it may have learned that annotator's style. Evaluate against the other annotator or a consensus.
:::

---

**Q7.** A recall of 0.9 is measured on 300 objects, all from 3 images. Is $\pm 2\sqrt{0.9 \cdot 0.1/300} = \pm 0.035$ a fair uncertainty?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Are the 300 objects independent?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No, it is too optimistic. The formula assumes 300 independent objects, but objects of one image share its illumination, density and staining. If the method does badly on one image, a whole block of objects fails at once. The real uncertainty is closer to that of a handful of images; evaluate per image and use more images and experiments.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that if auto $= 0.8 \cdot$ manual exactly, the Bland–Altman points lie on a line through the origin with slope $-2/9$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write the difference and the mean in terms of the manual value $x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$d = 0.8x - x = -0.2x$ and $m = (x + 0.8x)/2 = 0.9x$, so $d = (-0.2/0.9)\,m = -\frac29 m$.
:::
